items.title: Apple may adopt 'sputtering' OLED manufacture for brighter displays
items.content_html:
Apple's suppliers are working on a new OLED manufacturing technology that could deliver brighter displays for the iPhone and iPad.

Apple has long planned to replace the displays on all of its products with OLED. While it is well on its way to achieving that goal, the OLED panels it uses in the future could be a marked improvement over what's in use now.

According to The Elec on November 3, Apple display suppliers Samsung Display and LG Display are working on new methods to make OLED screens. Both are suppliers in Apple's OLED supply chain, and are keen to secure more orders from the company.

A source says that Apple is prioritizing the use of an existing sputtering process for creating High Mobility Oxide (HMO) based panels. Both Samsung and LG are creating new Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) and sputtering methods they can use on production lines.

There are a few advantages to the changes, including brighter individual pixels on the panel. This can increase not only the brightness but also affect the contrast of the screens.

The research may also make the cost per display a little bit cheaper, making it more suitable for use on budget-friendly products.

HMO, ALD, and Sputtering

HMO refers to a process that makes the thin-film transistor (TFT) used to turn an pixel on and off better. As the "High Mobility" bit of the name indicates, electrons in that circuit move three to five times faster than normal.

This helps the creation of high refresh rate displays, which are needed for features like ProMotion.

Both Sputtering and ALD refer to deposition technologies, or how the OLED material is applied to the thin-film substrate in the first place.

Sputtering relies on plasma to detach atoms from a material and to deposit them to the substrate. It's a useful technology, as it can use equipment already in use on OLED production lines, so there's little need to acquire more specialized hardware.


The PROLED MacBook Pro apparently uses HMO, but sputtering and ALD could result in an even better display - Image Credit: Apple

ALD uses gaseous materials, which are then applied to the layer directly. This is a very highly controllable process since layer thickness can be precisely managed, and therefore define the layer's electrical characteristics.

However, unlike sputtering, ALD does require high-cost machinery and raw materials. That accuracy has a considerable cost.

As a result, both Samsung Display and LG are prioritizing the development of sputtering, while also researching ALD in the background, one source claims.

The future is now

Though the report is all about the display suppliers researching and developing the technology, it may already be here.

According to RDL advisor and former DSCC CEO Ross Young, the new PROLED MacBook Pro is already using HMO for its display panel. It doesn't use existing LTPS or LTPO technologies for its backplane.

The manufacturing of the panel is allegedly performed on Samsung's A6 fab, which is the first in the industry to produce displays with HMO. Young adds that the panels are made using a much larger substrate than current LTPO and LTPS production lines.

While the display is interesting for using HMO, it's not one that uses sputtering nor ALD. When either of those get approved and adopted by Apple, it may get even better than the PROLED MacBook Pro's screen.

items.title: When to watch "A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving" for free on Apple TV
items.content_html:
Find something to be thankful for with the holiday classic "A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving." Here's how and, crucially, when you can watch it for free on Apple TV.

It's been more than 50 years since Charlie Brown and his friends first gathered around the Thanksgiving table. In that time, they've become a part of countless yearly traditions for families across America.

That's why Apple TV is giving everyone two all-access days to tune in. Anyone can watch "A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving" for free on Saturday, November 14, and Sunday, November 15.

Apple TV subscribers can watch for free at any time.

Charlie Brown, Snoopy, and friends will also return for the classic "A Charlie Brown Christmas" in December.

You have plenty of options to stream Peanuts specials along with the rest of Apple TV's catalog. If you've already got an Apple device, the easiest way is through Apple's official apps, including the one on the iPhone.

You can also watch through the Apple TV set-top box or on most smart TVs. Modern browsers let users stream Apple TV from any platform, making it the easiest option for those without Apple devices.

How to watch "A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving" for free on Apple TV in 2026

  1. In any modern web browser, go to tv.apple.com
  2. Log into your iCloud account or make a new one
  3. Find the show and press Play
  4. Watch it on your computer or stream it to a television of your choice

Only on Apple TV

In 2020, Apple signed a deal with rights holders WildBrain and Peanuts Worldwide to bring Snoopy, Charlie Brown, and the whole gang to Apple TV. In October 2025, the company announced an extension of that deal.

Apple TV holds exclusive streaming rights to all Peanuts content through 2030. Watching new or classic specials outside limited streaming windows requires an Apple TV subscription.

Apple TV offers a free, three-month trial when a first-time watcher buys a qualifying device, such as an iPhone. If you haven't purchased an iPhone and have not tried Apple TV yet, you may be eligible for a seven-day trial.

After the trial ends, the monthly cost is $14.99, or $119.99 per year.

items.title: Supreme Court won't hear Apple & Epic's case until January 2027
items.content_html:
The Supreme Court has convened for its October session only to tell Apple that it and Epic would be making their arguments heard in 2027 while battles in the lower courts continue.

Apple can't seem to catch a break as the Supreme Court pushes the timeline back further for potentially rendering Epic's remaining case moot. The argument being made to the Supreme Court deals with the lower court's ability to declare something a violation in the "spirit" of the law.

According to a note posted to the Supreme Court's website, first spotted by 9to5Mac, the Supreme Court will hear Apple and Epic's arguments on January 11, 2027. Unlike previous updates, this is a concrete date that at least indicates things are moving forward.

While both companies have repeatedly made their case known in various filings, this will be their chance to have it placed in the official record in front of the court. There is no telling whether or not the Supreme Court will render judgement in January or push that off to a later session in 2027.

After a lengthy Apple vs Epic trial, Epic lost on nearly every count except one forcing Apple to end its anti-steering practices. The court then found Apple in violation of this order, and Apple has been battling the decision ever since.

Apple challenged the injunction violation on two counts — that a violation must be found based on the letter of the law, not the spirit, and that the CASA case would limit the scope of the court's ability to render an injunction. The Supreme Court tossed the CASA argument, but will be hearing Apple's case on the injunction violation basis.

Repeated filings and amicus briefs have argued that the Supreme Court must overturn the decision, as every other court except the Ninth Circuit bases its decisions on the letter of the law. Apple's order to end anti-steering didn't mention how it should handle commissions, yet the court argued that Apple's implementation of fees violated the injunction's spirit.

There is no telling how the Supreme Court will rule, or when.

items.title: TerraMaster D1 SSD Pro review: Faster than my Mac's internal storage
items.content_html: With Apple OS, a huge external hard drive or NVME M.2 SSD can be added to a M2, M4, M6 computer. However, unlike a PC, the software has to reside on the internal drive with the OS. Storage and memory in Apple computers is seriously proprietary and costly. The customer has to choose more internal storage space than they would with a PC before the purchase so the internal SSD doesn't run out of space. You cannot load software programs externally only the data connected to programs. On a PC with an external drive, programs can be installed and data stored on that drive leaving the OS drive alone. An external larger than life drive for Apple is only good for photos and file storage. There is cumbersome work around, but it's a confusing manipulating mess. Apple stresses reliability and consistency in their design and I am sure that is why they keep their design tightly controlled. If your buying an Apple computer, purchase double the memory and storage space or you will regret your choice later.

items.title: Apple's latest giant education deal: 170,000 MacBook Neo to Philippines
items.content_html:
Apple's budget-friendly MacBook Neo is seeing big success in the global education market, with 170,000 units sold to teachers and school staff members in the Philippines.

Announced in March 2026, the MacBook Neo is the first Apple laptop powered by an iPhone chip: the A18 Pro. Though initially priced at $499 for the education market, Apple raised the price to $649 in late October 2026.

Recent price increases aside, the MacBook Neo remains the cheapest MacBook that can be purchased from Apple. As such, it only makes sense that the low-cost laptop found a significant customer base among educators, especially in emerging markets.

During Apple's quarterly earnings call, held on Monday, the company revealed it had sold 170,000 MacBook Neo units to teachers and school staff members in the Philippines. This is one of Apple's most significant education deals and serves to highlight the success of the MacBook Neo.

"We recently secured our biggest education deal ever for Mac with the Department of Education in the Philippines," said Apple CEO John Ternus. "They're going to deploy 170,000 MacBook Neos to teachers and staff."

"Opportunities like this bring more users into our ecosystem and help fuel growth across our business," Ternus added. In the Philippines, the 256GB MacBook Neo is priced at roughly $721.25 for the education market, with the 512GB model going for approximately $837.

As for Apple's overall Q4 2026 financial results, the company's revenue amounted to $114.5 billion, up from $102.5 billion during the same quarter in 2025.

items.title: Nevermind, AAPL is down after earnings
items.content_html:
That is because investors think about the future not the past and financial calls are in essence about the past.

If both show no upsides it get's bad. Apple's gross margin dropped significantly (even though they raised their sale prices) and they are warning about high component prices continuing. (and let's face it since they are no longer TSMCs number 1 customer by volume I would assume they will rise their prices as well)

On top of that we have a lackluster product portfolio and nothing really innovative (let's face it VR is a dud) and even the oh so promising service revenue did no longer grow by 2-digit numbers. So the high P/E ratio is harder to justify. (Admittedly expecting that that Apple delivers more than hooray propaganda in the financial call is preposterous to begin with).

items.title: Nevermind, AAPL is down after earnings
items.content_html: It took until the conclusion of the live stream, but investors are back to their goofy patterns. Despite the massive quarter, and expectations of about $148 billion in the next, A big sell-off happened in the seconds after the conference call. AAPL is down $8.79 per share as of 5:30 ET.

items.title: Apple's earnings were all about unprecedented memory costs
items.content_html:
A constant issue throughout Apple's latest earnings call was the cost of memory. John Ternus warned several times that the company has only a few ways to minimize the impact for consumers.

Even as Apple reported better than expected results in its Q4 earnings call, both Ternus and Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh cautioned analysts about the problems of high memory prices.

"Let me give you an overall view on memory," John Ternus said. "What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented. And as we said earlier in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carry-in inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components."

Carry-in is when a company like Apple increases production to build up inventory ahead of price rises. Apple successfully did this when Trump's "reciprocal" tariffs were introduced, and Ternus is admitting that the firm is trying to continue the practice.

But there is a limit to how much can be physically produced. Ternus, and the rest of the industry, believes that price hikes by RAM suppliers are far from over.

What happens next

"Now, for the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs, partly offset by a few factors," he said. "So as you know, we changed the price on many of our products, including Mac and iPad at the end of June, and iPhone in September, and these pricing increases provided some offset."

He repeated that there would be some savings because of getting lower costs on other components. Plus there will still be some carry-in benefit even in December.

"Looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase," said Ternus. "As we said before, we do believe we'll see a decreasing benefit from the carry-in inventory on memory over time."

Alongside painting this picture for how Apple will be affected in the foreseeable future, Ternus and Parekh both repeatedly referred to the impact of memory costs on this quarter's results. Mostly, because the analysts on the call asked the same question over and over, just using different words.

But to at least try leaving the topic on a more positive point, Ternus said that he wanted to add what Apple is doing "as we work to improve supply." He said that building up US production was part of this, referring to Apple's American Manufacturing Program.

But, none of that spend is towards RAM and flash media.

items.title: Over 2.5 billion daily Siri requests put Apple's AI overhaul in perspective
items.content_html:
Siri handles more than 2.5 billion requests a day, a figure Apple revisited during its November earnings discussion as it works to make the assistant more capable with AI.

CEO John Ternus repeated the number as Apple reported its fiscal fourth-quarter results, although the milestone isn't new. Lilian Rincon, Apple's vice president of product marketing for artificial intelligence, first revealed it during the September 9 iPhone event.

At WWDC 2024, Apple reported that Siri handled 1.5 billion voice requests daily. The newer figure is more than 1 billion higher, but the company hasn't said whether the two numbers measure the same kinds of interactions.

Apple's 2024 figure counted voice requests, while its newer figure of 2.5 billion daily Siri requests doesn't specify exactly what's included. Without a consistent definition, it's difficult to tell how much Siri usage has actually grown.

Meanwhile, Apple has been rolling out its Siri AI overhaul, which began reaching customers in September with iOS 27. The redesigned assistant uses Apple Intelligence to understand personal context, handle more complicated questions, and take actions across apps.

Siri can also pull information from messages, emails, and photos, so users don't have to remember exactly where they saved something or which conversation contained a particular detail.

The new features aren't available to everyone yet. Siri AI remains in beta, and eligible users must join a waitlist before gaining access. Some features that depend on server-based AI models also have daily usage limits, with broader access expected to require payment eventually.

Apple has gradually expanded availability, adding five languages on October 26. Siri AI now supports French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish alongside English, although regional restrictions still apply.

The 2.5 billion daily requests also include traditional Siri interactions, such as setting alarms, sending messages, and controlling smart-home devices. Apple hasn't revealed how many people are using the newer AI features or what share of daily requests they account for.

items.title: John Ternus enthuses about Apple's future on his first earnings call
items.content_html:
Apple CEO John Ternus - image credit: Apple.

As Tim Cook did when he took over, new Apple CEO John Ternus took several minutes out of his first earnings call with analysts and shareholders to say why he feels great about the state of the company and its future.

As Apple reported better than expected earnings for the firm's fourth-quarter financial results, Ternus claimed that it is "the greatest company in the world." Unsurprisingly, he touted Apple's newest devices and their features, but he did also speak more broadly about the company.

It's a privilege to be with you for the first time as Apple CEO. I'm honoured to represent our teams and the work they do every day. This is an amazing time at Apple. We just completed one of the most prolific launch periods in our history. It's been a remarkable time for innovation across all of our categories. Apple is the greatest company in the world. We've assembled an extraordinary collection of talent. The best engineers, designers, developers, and experts in every corner of our business. From our supply chain to our stores.
Every day, we bring the right people together with the best ideas to build products and services that change lives. Guided by a foundational set of values and a belief that the best technology should make a better world. We do that by making products that are powerful and intuitive, and meet Apple's uncompromising standards for quality, performance, design, and durability.
That's the Apple experience customers love. And with our latest lineup, people have even more reasons than ever to upgrade or switch to an Apple product. At the same time, Apple Services amplify the experience of every device.
Ultimately, everything we do at Apple is for our users. The success of every innovation is best measured by its impact on people's lives. And that's what drives us to keep building great products and to get them into the hands of people all around the world.

Ternus's view of Apple and its future

John Ternus walked shareholders through highlights in Apple's financial quarter, but then he also talked more generally about the company. He said that he was proud of what Apple had achieved both for users and for American manufacturing.

People love Apple products and services for the countless ways they make life easier, more enjoyable, and just plain better. They also count on Apple to create technology responsibly, built the right way, not the easy way. That means building products with even more recycled content to take less from the earth, and with even better durability, so they last longer.
It means developing intelligent capabilities like sound recognition on Apple Watch to alert users who are deaf or hard of hearing to what's happening around them. It means designing privacy protections like on-device processing so personal data stays on a user's device, and it means introducing new child safety features to make it easier for parents to manage when and how their kids can use their devices.
We're also pleased to be doing more and more manufacturing in the United States. Through our American manufacturing program, we're deepening partnerships with suppliers across the country, including Peeryman, a titanium producer now supplying iPhone Duo, and Qnity Electronics, which is producing the camera technology behind iPhone 18 Pro's new variable aperture system.
Nearly 100 components in our newest iPhones come from Paramin. American companies in more than a dozen states. All told, Apple supports more than 450,000 American jobs with thousands of suppliers and partners across all 50 states. It's all part of our $600 billion four-year commitment to U.S. innovation and advanced manufacturing.
I am proud of what we've accomplished this quarter, and I'm excited for what's ahead. We have everything we need to be extraordinarily successful, and with this team, this vision, this mission, and these values, I have no doubt that we will.

When Apple uses earnings calls to say more

Apple's earning calls are one hour per quarter, in which the company recites the same figures it announces in its financial filings. The CEO and CFO also then take questions, though a great many of those questions are about future products or plans, and so they are not answered.

There have been times, though, when the basic format of the call has been altered. Before Ternus's first call, for instance, there was Tim Cook's last one. In that, Cook talked about the transition of CEO, and thanked shareholders for their support.

Cook also broke the format back in October 2011. As he said at the time, that was the first Apple earnings call following the death of co-founder Steve Jobs.

"The world has lost a visionary, a creative genius, and an amazing human being," Cook said. "His spirit will forever be the foundation of Apple."

items.title: Over 2.5 billion active devices gives Apple Services a massive audience
items.content_html:
Apple's installed base has surpassed 2.5 billion active devices worldwide, CEO John Ternus confirmed during the company's November 2 earnings call, with the total reaching another record across all major product categories and regions.

Ternus reiterated the 2.5 billion figure while discussing Apple's fiscal fourth-quarter results. Although the installed base continues to grow, the company didn't provide a more precise updated device count.

Apple first surpassed 2.5 billion devices in January 2026, up roughly 150 million from the 2.35 billion reported in 2025.

The installed base includes active iPhones, iPads, Macs, Apple Watches, and other products. It measures devices rather than individual customers, meaning someone who owns multiple Apple products contributes more than one device to the total.

Apple's growing device base supports Services revenue

The expanding installed base gives Apple a larger potential audience for Services, including iCloud, Apple Music, Apple TV, and the App Store. Unlike hardware purchases, subscriptions and other digital services can generate revenue long after customers buy their devices.

Services revenue reached a record $31.57 billion during the September quarter, up nearly 10% from $28.75 billion a year earlier. Apple's latest earnings also showed total revenue climbing 12% to $114.5 billion, while iPhone revenue reached a September-quarter record of $57.58 billion.

In July, Apple reported more than 1.5 billion paid subscriptions across its platform, including Apple's own services and third-party offerings.

The figure represents subscriptions rather than individual customers, so it doesn't directly correspond to the number of active devices. The growing installed base provides a foundation for future Services revenue, but Apple hasn't disclosed which products contributed most to its latest increase.

items.title: Apple still can't meet iPhone Duo demand, and Ternus won't say when it will
items.content_html:
John Ternus marked his first earnings as Apple CEO with iPhone Duo shortages and a rebuilt Siri taking center stage. He's vague about when Apple will make enough iPhone Duo units, though.

Apple CEO John Ternus has addressed supply constraints and display concerns surrounding the company's first foldable iPhone. He also discussed the rebuilt Siri, which now handles 2.5 billion requests daily.

The iPhone Duo sold out quickly online and drew lines at Apple stores in October. Apple is increasing efforts to meet demand.

"Duo is constrained as of today," Ternus told Reuters. "The ramp is going well, and we're working hard to get it to as many customers as quickly as possible, but at this point, we're not able to predict when supply and demand will be in balance."

Some iPhone Duo customers have reported cracked screens since the device launched. Ternus said "a very small percentage" of devices had been returned for display issues. Apple is replacing affected units.

An AI-driven surge in memory demand has pushed component costs higher. Apple recently raised iPhone 17 prices by $100 and increased MacBook prices.

"We did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which was partially offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components," Ternus told Reuters. "These price increases provided some offset."

Ternus also reflected on Apple's ambitions for its revamped voice assistant. The new, more personal Siri was initially slated for release in 2024 and faced repeated delays.

"Now we have the Siri that we always wanted, which we really built from the ground up," Ternus said.

Apple reported its Q4 earnings on Monday, November 2. The quarter earned $114.5 billion.

items.title: Apple keeps its $0.27 dividend payout unchanged
items.content_html:
Apple shareholders will receive another $0.27 per share on November 16, keeping the quarterly cash dividend unchanged following a record September quarter.

The company's board of directors approved the payment alongside its fiscal fourth-quarter earnings results on Monday. Shareholders of record as of the close of business on November 12, 2026, will be eligible for the dividend.

The payout continues the $0.27 rate Apple maintained in July, following a 4% increase from $0.26 to $0.27 per share in April 2026.

For shareholders, the payment works out to $27 for every 100 shares owned before any applicable taxes. If Apple maintains the current rate for four quarters, the annual dividend would total $1.08 per share.

Quarterly diluted EPS and dividend, as of Q4 2026

The dividend comes alongside Apple's latest earnings, which showed quarterly revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12% year over year. Diluted earnings per share rose 14% to $2.10, while iPhone revenue set a September-quarter record and Services reached a new all-time high.

Apple generated $28 billion in operating cash flow during the quarter and returned $28 billion to shareholders through dividends and other capital returns, including share repurchases.

The company's dividend remains a relatively small part of its shareholder returns. During fiscal 2026, the company spent $86.4 billion repurchasing shares, compared with $15.7 billion on dividends and dividend equivalents.

The difference shows how heavily Apple's capital return program favors stock buybacks over direct cash payments.

The dividend represents a direct cash payment to investors, separate from Apple's stock buyback activity. It continues the company's policy of returning capital to shareholders.

items.title: Apple's record-breaking Q4 beat Covid-fueled 2020 holiday quarter
items.content_html:
In spite of not releasing the lower-priced base iPhone 18 model, Apple's Q4 2026 has broken records and beat out what was seen as an unprecedented holiday quarter just a few years ago.

iPhone 18 Pro didn't need the base model to help Apple break records

Pundits continue to be confused by Apple's repeat record-breaking quarters in spite of not building its own AI frontier model. Instead, Apple has reached new revenue highs on iPhone demand, superior Mac hardware, and continued innovation across its product lines.

While Q4 2026 isn't what you'd call a "blow away," it is a year-over-year increase in revenue at $114.5 billion. That number would have been considered incredible for a holiday quarter just a few years ago -- handily beating the Covid-fueled $111.4 billion earned in Q1 2021.

Revenue was also helped by higher prices across Apple's product lines. The increased revenues are likely obfuscating unit shipment changes that are less ideal.

That said, CEO John Ternus did reveal that Apple has sold more Macs in the calendar year than ever before.

Apple quarterly revenue and gross margin from 2018 to 2026

What might be even more interesting about the record-breaking Q4 is what is missing in this report. New Macs, iPhone Duo, and Apple's new Apple Home push did not launch during Q4.

While Apple beat Wall Street expectation in Q4, all eyes are on the 2027 Q1 earnings that will arrive just as the world cools off on AI. The company's push for vertical integration of hardware and software with private, local-first, and secure AI could mean it's among the biggest winners in the AI race.

items.title: Sunday Reboot: Sam Altman needs to read the RAM room
items.content_html:
In this week's Sunday Reboot, Sam Altman thinks it's wasteful for you to have more memory in your Mac. It's bad enough that you have any RAM that he can't access at all.

Sunday Reboot is a weekly column covering some of the lighter stories within the Apple reality distortion field from the past seven days. All to get next week underway with a good first step.

Blissful unawareness

When it comes to CEO pronouncements, they can be a mixed bag. Comments like Nvidia's Jensen Huang being fine with paying a billionaire tax are good ones, giving brief moments of hope that the 1% isn't entirely full of out-of-touch rich people.

For the moment at least, John Ternus hasn't fallen into the trap of uttering something damaging to the heavily managed Apple CEO persona. It's early days in his tenure, so there's still plenty of time for that to happen.

That said, there are plenty of company leaders who are outspoken and provide a controversial point of view. Lots of lessons on how not to conduct yourself as a figurehead for Ternus to absorb.

The latest one is from Sam Altman, the guy in charge over at OpenAI, which operates the current AI heavyweight ChatGPT.

I'm not talking about anything to do with the whole Jony Ive hardware thing nor the related lawsuit. Nor the tone-deaf response to AI hacking that OpenAI's tools are being used to both facilitate and protect against.

This time, it's memory. The computing component that has skyrocketed in price to be more precious than printer ink, thanks to AI's Borg-like need to consume it all.

Sam Altman in a pub. Or more likely, a pub set. - Image Credit: Cheeky Pint/YouTube

In the latest tone-deaf pronouncement, speaking to YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, Altman lamented that there's not enough memory for AI. Apparently, end users are the problem.

"From a global allocation perspective, it's quite terrible to have, like, everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer," Altman declared. In his estimation, it's only being used about "5% of the time."

He says that there should be "maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that."

Translated, he's saying that the memory used in your Mac would be better used as part of the almighty AI machine to serve you indirectly.

He almost has a point

The immediate knee-jerk reaction is that he's wrong, with the emotional side of all of us silently screaming horrible things at him.

Maybe paraphrasing Braveheart by declaring, "You may take our money, but you'll never take our memory." Maybe he's somehow affected by being in a set that is made to look like a sociable environment and not the robot side of The Matrix.

Before we get to that, as distasteful as it is, let's play devil's advocate for a moment and see his side.

Altman [right] and Jony Ive [left] at a different bar. - Image Credit: OpenAI

To him, the memory market is tough, with many people wanting flash chips and willing to pay for them. If we plebeian users just didn't buy any more memory, there would be more available for OpenAI and every other AI company to suck up and spit out into their infrastructure projects.

This is a logic that almost makes sense, but only if you take his point of view. You're invested and infatuated with the progress forward of AI, and that's your single-minded goal in life.

Of course you're not going to care about someone being able to afford the more expensive PlayStation 5 to play Grand Theft Auto 6. That's a waste of resources, when the memory in that game console could be used to further humanity by letting a computer think on its behalf.

This is, to me, the Star Trek fantasy. War between countries has become a "solved problem," and everyone is now working together in harmony for the greater good, often against their best interests.

Almost

Stepping out of the role of Lucifer's care worker, the argument falls flat in many different ways.

For a start, the memory industry is already leaning heavily in favor of the Great AI Industrial Machine. The major memory producers have already shifted production capacity towards data center-grade High Bandwidth Memory, cutting the amount of DRAM to go around.

Data centers are already taking a massive cut of DRAM sales, along with device producers, with direct-to-consumer and business memory sales being an afterthought. Indeed, competition is so high that, even with stratospheric memory pricing, the 2027 supply pipeline is already booked solid.

Since it's so expensive that consumers have to seriously consider how much memory their new purchases contain, Altman already has his wish. AI's buying most of the new memory anyway, and will for some time.

Anyone wanting to buy a new Mac from Apple is having the same thoughts about whether they can live without more RAM or if it's viable going into the second-hand organ sales trade.

Sam Altman. Presumably, the bar has been swallowed by a void, leaving Altman alone with his thoughts about wearing brown shirts all the time. - Image credit: Emerson Collective

In my particular case, I did upgrade my gaming PC earlier in the year. However, because RAM pricing was so goddamned high, the new build was centered around my existing DDR4 memory instead of buying new DDR5, or even increasing the amount of memory in use.

Even with investments by memory companies into new infrastructure, that's going to make only a small dent in the issue, and it will take too long. AI will also consume that, too.

To consumers, it's clear that AI infrastructure buildouts are the reason why there's so much memory demand in the first place. It's a problem that OpenAI and others have no real right to complain about, because their actions caused this situation in the first place.

We can't even propose that OpenAI starts its own memory manufacturing effort so it can secure a private supply of chips to its particular specifications. The problem is, if you're spending extremely high amounts of cash to do that, the easier option would be to buy out an existing memory producer altogether.

Thankfully, that's not a possibility for the moment, since the big three memory makers have extremely high values, thanks to this very problem of supply and demand. Namely they're benefiting from the rest of the tech manufacturing industry's misery.

At this point, Altman's comments are annoying, effectively taunting an angry tech industry and budget-conscious users because AI is consuming almost everything, and it's not satisfied.

It may be an altruistic proposal for the good of humankind's future to Altman. To everyone else, it's a misguided statement that ignores everyone else's deep unhappiness due to all electronics increasing in price as a result.

Maybe Sam truly doesn't see how his comment plays to observers because he's so invested in his own AI bubble. To me, I can't decide between imagining him as the Grinch or Blofeld.

Last week's Sunday Reboot discussed the Apple Music rebrand's physical coolness, as well as stupidity in security.

items.title: Apple's received most of its Trump reciprocal tariff refunds
items.content_html:
Apple has received most of what it paid to the U.S. government in extra tariffs back, which marginally helped to improve the Q4 results.

Back in June, Apple benefited from approximately $2.2 billion in tariff refunds, getting funds back from the 'reciprocal' tariffs that were shut down by the Supreme Court in February. Apple had another payment that affects its fourth-quarter results.

In its quarterly results for Q4, Apple says that the 47.9% gross margin included a "favorable impact" of approximately 1% thanks to the tariff refunds. Similarly, approximately $0.05 of the $2.10 diluted earnings per share stemmed from the refunds.

Apple doesn't say how much the tariff refunds make up, but some simple math puts it in the ballpark of a billion dollars.

As for whether this windfall will continue, there may be some action, but not as much as people may think. During the conference call to analysts, chief financial officer Kevan Parekh confirmed that the vast majority of tariff refunds have been paid back to Apple.

There may be a bit more to come, but certainly not at the billion-dollar level.

items.title: Apple beats Wall Street forecasts in first Ternus-led Q4 earnings
items.content_html:
The fourth-quarter financial results for 2026 have arrived, the first under new CEO John Ternus, with Apple's revenue of $114.5 billion.

The Q4 results bring Apple's financial year to an end, one that has been massively transitional for the company. It's the first results under the watchful eye of John Ternus, following Tim Cook's last results call in July.

It was a quarter that also involved many product launches, including the new iPhone 18 Pro models, updates to the Mac lineup, a smart home refresh, and the iPhone Duo. The full financial effect of those product launches will be felt in the upcoming Q1 results.

Apple quarterly revenue and gross margin, as of Q4 2026

For Q4, Apple achieved revenue of $114.5 billion, up from the $102.5 billion reported in Q4 2025. The Wall Street consensus was $113.4 billion.

When it comes to product categories, the iPhone revenue of $57.58 billion is up from the $54.25 billion of Q4 2025. Mac revenue went from $10.35 billion in the year-ago quarter to $10.79 billion in the latest quarter.

The iPad revenue of $6.23 billion is up from $6.19 billion for Q4 2025. Wearables, Home, and Accessories saw revenue shift from $7.88 billion last year to $8.3 billion.

Services, the consistent growth center in the financial results, continued its steady upward march from $30.73 billion in Q4 2025 to $31.57 billion in Q4 2026.

Apple revenue by unit, as of Q4 2026

As it is the last quarter of the financial year, Apple has also reported its full-year figures.

Gross sales of $478.3 billion are up from the $416.2 billion reported for the 2025 financial year. The gross margin has also gone up, from $195.2 billion in 2025 to $233.6 billion in 2026.

Apple annual revenue, gross margin, and net income as of Q4 2026

Ternus referred to Apple achieving a new September quarter record and Services hitting an all-time high. It's also the best fiscal year for the company.

Along with launches like the iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, and the touch-enabled MacBook Pro, "it's an incredible lineup to carry us into the holiday season," he said.

items.title: Apple keeps its $0.27 dividend payout unchanged
items.content_html:
Apple shareholders will receive another $0.27 per share on November 16, keeping the quarterly cash dividend unchanged following a record September quarter.

The company's board of directors approved the payment alongside its fiscal fourth-quarter earnings results on Monday. Shareholders of record as of the close of business on November 12, 2026, will be eligible for the dividend.

The payout continues the $0.27 rate Apple maintained in July, following a 4% increase from $0.26 to $0.27 per share in April 2026.

For shareholders, the payment works out to $27 for every 100 shares owned before any applicable taxes. If Apple maintains the current rate for four quarters, the annual dividend would total $1.08 per share.


Quarterly diluted EPS and dividend, as of Q4 2026

The dividend comes alongside Apple's latest earnings, which showed quarterly revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12% year over year. Diluted earnings per share rose 14% to $2.10, while iPhone revenue set a September-quarter record and Services reached a new all-time high.

Apple generated $28 billion in operating cash flow during the quarter and returned $28 billion to shareholders through dividends and other capital returns, including share repurchases.

The company's dividend remains a relatively small part of its shareholder returns. During fiscal 2026, the company spent $86.4 billion repurchasing shares, compared with $15.7 billion on dividends and dividend equivalents.

The difference shows how heavily Apple's capital return program favors stock buybacks over direct cash payments.

The dividend represents a direct cash payment to investors, separate from Apple's stock buyback activity. It continues the company's policy of returning capital to shareholders.

items.title: Apple promotes Labrinth stream just ahead of OLED MacBook Pro release
items.content_html:
Apple will be holding a special stream with musician Labrinth on November 4, in a "Live on Mac" performance.

When you hear of Apple holding a stream with a musical artist, it's usually under the purview of Apple Music. However, one online event Apple is promoting seems to be all about the music creation process itself.

In a TikTok post on November 2, a video shows a white box slid into frame, complete with the label "Do not touch until 11.04.26." A hand comes in from one side, scrawling "For Labrinth" on the top, before hauling it away.

The post itself includes the date as well as the time of 8pm PST, as well as mentioning it will be "Live on YouTube" with the link in the TikTok account's bio.

That link takes you to the YouTube page for an upcoming stream on Labrinth's YouTube account, with an image showing "Labrinth Live on Mac" with the date and time. The description for the stream says he will be "Experimenting with some new ways of making music."

Labrinth is a prolific singer, songwriter, composer, and record producer, being involved in sounds such as "Pass Out" and "Beneath Your Beautiful." He has worked with artists including Beyonce, Rihanna, Nikki Minaj, and Eminem, as well as the the soundtrack for "The Lion King: The Gift."

Given the release date of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED display is for November 6, it's almost certainly going to be a stream promoting the new touchscreen, and maybe Logic enhancements, especially considering the size of the TikTok video's package.

items.title: Hands on: HomePod mini 2 has promise, but is underwhelming right now
items.content_html:
The new $149 HomePod mini 2 is finally available six years after the last model shopped. While it shows some promise, there's just not enough here yet.

You'd be hard-pressed to differentiate the new HomePod mini 2 from the original. Put the Midnight or white models side-by-side and they're indistinguishable.

Physically, the only thing that sets them apart is the logo on the bottom. It's no longer printed, but is now molded into the rubber footing.

It's easier to differentiate if you have one of the new colors. Aside from Midnight and white, the HomePod mini 2 also comes in a slightly lighter blue, as well as pink and green.

Personally, I love the new green color, but I wish some of the other ones stuck around. I would have been thrilled if we had another orange model or a dark red.

HomePod mini 2 has a dual-color mesh

The new colors have this dual-color 3D mesh, which is cooler when you get up close. On the green, the underlying layer is blue and is a subtle design accent to appreciate.

After picking up a green model for myself, I have been testing it the last couple of days in my home. Let's see how it compares to my original HomePod minis.

Noticeably faster

The biggest thing I noticed with the new HomePod mini 2 is how fast it is. Apple upgraded it from the S5 processor to the S10.

Hand Off is much quicker on the HomePod mini 2

Handoff and Siri answers are much faster on the updated speaker. It makes it nicer to use and it gives a sense of responsiveness that it didn't have before.

Quite often I felt like the old HomePod mini just spun its wheels processing my requests. This isn't reason enough alone to warrant an upgrade, but it's very nice.

The other internal change with the HomePod mini 2 is improved wireless. It has both Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 6.

Speaker pairing

There are two new pairing options for the HomePod mini 2. This little speaker can serve as a dedicated output for your Mac or in a four-speaker array on Apple TV 4K.

The former is limited to Macs that support Wi-Fi 6E or newer while the latter is restricted to the new fourth-generation Apple TV 4K. Since the new Apple TV 4K isn't out yet, I didn't get a chance to test this at home.

HomePod mini 2 next to the Apple TV 4K

I did get several opportunities to listen to this at the Apple experience in NYC when the speaker was announced. Compared to only two HomePods, the sound was absolutely more immersive and room-filling.

Your own experience will vary though, and depends on your home. I don't have a lot of great locations to test this, so I don't think I'm going to be setting up a four-HomePod array permanently.

After trying it at the NYC experience, I wanted to try the Mac output, but wasn't able to. Even after updating my MacBook Pro and HomePod mini 2 to the latest 27.2 release, the option didn't present itself.

HomePod mini 2 and a green iMac

My audio settings still set the speaker up as a regular AirPlay audio destination, versus a dedicated output that would have no delay and play system sounds. Hopefully this gets resolved as a minor early bug.

We could have had more

Here's where I stand: I like the HomePod mini 2. It's a solid speaker and the green looks fantastic to me.

Underside of the HomePod mini 2

The speed improvement is huge, especially for smart home commands. Lights and other accessories respond right away when I control them via the speaker.

Sound Glow on HomePod mini matches the colors on the speaker to the album artwork

Another new feature, Sound Glow, is slick, but it comes to the old model too. Sound Glow changes the lights on top of the speaker to match the album art of what you're listening to.

I think I just wanted more after all this time. There's no change in audio quality, no updated top display, and the flagship feature isn't available here at launch.

Siri AI is the biggest change to HomePod mini 2 but it is coming "in a future software update." Apple didn't even provide guidance on when this update will arrive.

It could deliver with the upcoming 27.3 beta, or it could ship sometime in 2027. This is wild to me when Apple TV 4K, HomeView, and Apple Watch all got Siri AI before Apple's smart speaker.

After a few days, I'm enjoying the general quality of life improvements, but when I step back, it leaves me wanting more. My guess is my optimism will improve when Siri AI ships, but until then I'm slightly underwhelmed.

items.title: How your old Apple TV 4K is new again with tvOS 27.2 update
items.content_html:
Apple recently launched tvOS 27.2 which contains a swath of new features for existing Apple TV 4K users. Here's how your streaming box gets even better.

The new fourth-generation Apple TV 4K carries a hefty price tag, which is why the new tvOS 27.2 update is so welcomed. Existing users get several new features without buying a new box.

Many features are available now, though one big one is just around the corner.

Siri Remote

There's one quick and easy way to upgrade your existing Apple TV 4K, other than through updating its software. That's by picking up one of the newly-upgraded Siri Remotes, which is supported with tvOS 27.2.

The new Siri Remote has a built-in tone generator, so when you lose your remote, you can have it play back a chime. In my testing of the new Siri Remote at Apple's NYC experience, the chime helped greatly.

Even buried in the couch cushion you could hear the chirping from across the room. If you're too far away or the remote is too deeply buried, the remote supports Precision Finding.

Similar to an AirTag, you can use your iPhone or Apple Watch to get directional guidance to where the remote is located within inches. The latest Siri Remote is available from Apple for $59 and works all the way back to the Apple TV HD.

If you keep your existing Siri Remote, tvOS 27.2 finally brings it into the Find My app. That means you won't have to open the Remote app, go to the top drop-down, and hit find.

Instead, you'll venture to the Find My app where all your other trackable items are housed. That said, they don't get any new abilities, but it makes more sense to have one place to find all of your gadgets.

Screensavers

Apple has been expanding the screensavers for Apple TV 4K outside of its usual Aerial ones. There are no new ones here, but there is a new way to choose between them.

If you go into Settings > Screensavers, you can now turn on random. Every time your Apple TV 4K goes into sleep mode it will choose one of the available options including your photos, Aerial, Snoopy, and more.

I love this feature because we're always in debate about what screensaver to use, with the kids demanding Snoopy while I'm partial to the Aerial shots.

On the photo and memories screensavers, you can customize these using your iPhone or iPad. That way you don't have to add your entire library, but can choose specific photos that you want to cycle through.

Apple Music & Apple TV

Profiles for the Apple TV app are supported on iPhone and iPad with iOS 27.2, which is great for parents who may hand their device to a child to watch something. Profiles will make sure they don't see age-restricted content and what they watch won't impact your Watch Next queue.

Apple also added new customization for profile icons, allowing users to choose animated characters from some of Apple's shows. You can pick characters from Snoopy, Stillwater, and Frog and Toad.

The Apple Music app on Apple TV 4K has a new icon. It matches the rebrand across Apple's other platforms with a black background and white music note.

Within the Music app, artists can now upload custom logos, feature specific content, and choose their own accent colors.

Audio updates

Lastly, there are new audio improvements coming to Apple TV. Both American Sign Language (ASL) and British Sign Language (BSL) are supported.

If you visit Settings > TV > Sign Language, you can turn on either option. There's no indication which content it will work with, but it will be through the Apple TV streaming service.

Apple TV aficionado and Smart Home Insider guest Sigmund Judge noted that a receiver and HomePods can be used together for audio output. That unlocks the ability to use paired HomePods with a dedicated sub or high speakers.

It's a niche setup, but could be useful for those who want a bit more out of their HomePods. Ceiling-mounted high speakers would enable more precise Dolby Atmos.

More to come

For a mid-cycle update to Apple's set-top box, this is a substantial update. But Apple isn't done.

The tvOS 27.2 update also lays the groundwork for Siri AI. Apple has confirmed that Siri AI will be coming to the existing 3rd-generation Apple TV 4K soon as a beta.

Users can ask information about what they're watching (where was this scene filmed?), content from their messages or emails, and personalized recommendations. At launch, Siri AI will support English in eight countries, including the United States, Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa, and the United Kingdom.

items.title: Nine-inch HomeView Ultra again rumored for 2027 or 2028
items.content_html:
A further source has doubled down on rumors of Apple planning a larger HomeView, this time which can automatically swivel on its base.

It won't look like this, but a future HomeView is said to be larger than the current mode, and come on an articulated arm.

Even back in 2024, it was being reported that what would become the HomeView would be followed by a larger model. It was consistently also rumored that this version would have a robot-like arm that moved its screen 360 degrees to follow the user.

Now The Information is mostly repeating those rumors and also echoing more recent reports saying the larger model will launch in 2027. Where it differs is in that it believes it may be pushed back to 2028, and also that the hardware design has already "been finished for around two years."

The report also refers to a prototype being ready, which suggests that the device has not yet gone to manufacturing. It has previously been claimed that manufactured HomeView devices have been waiting years in warehouses for the release of the improved Siri AI before launching.

While this report doesn't go so far as to say hardware is waiting, it does claim that Apple actually began working on the project in 2019. Initially it was intended as a FaceTime device, but the idea of giving it a movable arm was followed by plans to add AI features to it.

Reportedly, there have been disagreements within Apple over the mix of software and hardware features in the initial release. While it's not known what those particular features are, they are reportedly being considered for a second or subsequent generation of the device.

Now this larger model is said to feature more cameras and sensors. So the arm could move to follow a user, with a greater range than Center Stage, but also be aware of obstructions.

The report says that the larger device may be called a HomeView Ultra or a HomeView Max. It is said to feature a nine-inch display, as compared to the six-inch one of the first model.

Reportedly, Apple is aiming to sell the larger HomeView for $1,000. The current first-generation model retails for $299.

Rumor Score: Possible

items.title: Cross-platform Affinity users can finally update as the app comes to the iPad
items.content_html:
A year after Canva revamped Affinity for the Mac, it has now released the free iPad version too. Not only is this good for iPad users, but it will free up some Mac ones to update as well.

Canva revamped the Affinity suite of publishing and illustration tools on the Mac back in 2025, but it wasn't backwards compatible. If you worked on both the Mac and the iPad, you couldn't update because the two platforms had to stay on the same version.

Now that's over as Canva has released Affinity for iPad. At times it's been referred to as Affinity Studio, but now it is simply Affinity on Mac, iPad, and Windows. It's not just the same name, though, as Canva claims that it has precisely the same features as the Mac version.

"Creative work doesn't stay in one discipline, so your tools shouldn't either," Duncan Clark, CEO of Pro Design at Canva, said in a statement. "Since we brought Affinity together on desktop, our biggest user request has been the desire to bring it to iPad. Today we're delivering it: a fully-fledged, professional app built for touch."

In AppleInsider's initial testing, it seems to be true that the full Affinity app has come to the iPad, but then it's not a surprise. What is now a single Canva Affinity app per platform, was previously a trio of Serif Affinity apps which AppleInsider was very familiar with.

With one click, Affinity users can switch between a full illustration app, a publishing one, or more. - image credit: Canva.

As well as being strong layout, photography, and illustration apps, those old Affinity Publisher, Affinity Photo, and Affinity Designer were notable for having identical Mac and iPad apps.

What's also the same between the Mac and the new iPad Affinity app is that they are both free for individual users. It caused huge concern for users when Canva first bought Affinity and then made it free.

But a year on from the Mac version being released, there's been no change to the pricing. And the iPad app has been developed further than its Serif predecessors.

Now when you first open Affinity on the iPad, it asks whether you are planning to use primarily touch or the Apple Pencil. And it introduces a Sketch Studio for freehand drawing.

The catch

If you're an individual user, there is no catch and you can just go download Affinity for iPad from the App Store right now. There is an in-app purchase that brings AI tools and templates, but none that are needed to use Affinity in full.

These subscription features do more closely link Canva's features to Affinity's. However, in a year producing half a dozen education magazines or publications, we've had no need to even look at what those extra tools are.

A personal subscription to what's called Canva Pro costs $18/month or $143.99/year. A business subscription for Affinity costs $250/year.

Affinity for iPad requires iPadOS 18 or greater. It runs on:

7th generation iPad or later

5th generation iPad mini or later

3rd generation iPad Air or later

All generations of 11-inch iPad Pro

3rd generation 12.9-inch iPad Pro

13-inch iPad Pro M4, M5 and later

items.title: Hundreds of AI apps were part of a network hiding sexually abusive deepfake tools
items.content_html:
Apple has removed 19 apps that concealed sexually abusive AI deepfake tools behind ordinary features after an investigation uncovered a network designed to evade App Store review.

A November 2 investigation identified more than 400 connected apps and web domains that appeared to offer harmless AI services, including pet portraits, language lessons, and fitness coaching. Some could instead load tools for generating sexually explicit images and videos using photographs of real people.

The findings build on earlier research showing that apps capable of creating nonconsensual sexual imagery were reaching the App Store despite Apple's restrictions. The newly uncovered network went further by using remote servers to control which features appeared to individual users.

How the apps concealed their true purpose

According to the WIRED investigation, researchers discovered that apps in the network contacted remote servers after installation. They transmitted information including the user's language, referral source, and a unique identifier.

The server decided whether to show the app's advertised features or load a separate website with explicit deepfake generators. Someone downloading the app normally might see nothing suspicious, while someone arriving through a particular advertisement could access the hidden tools.

One apparent trigger was downloading an app after clicking an advertisement on Facebook or Instagram. Researchers traced thousands of advertisements promoting sexually abusive deepfakes to apps distributed through Apple's App Store and Google Play.

One example was Viefur, an AI pet portrait generator that appeared to transform animal photographs into humanlike characters. Behind that harmless interface, researchers found access to tools capable of placing people into sexually explicit and violent scenarios.

Researchers also uncovered a JavaScript bundle containing references to hundreds of connected apps and domains, along with encryption keys and advertising trackers. The shared infrastructure indicated a coordinated operation rather than a collection of unrelated developers.

In September 2026, researchers identified 27 related apps on Google Play that had collectively accumulated more than 350,000 downloads. Many were rated suitable for all age groups, showing that the network extended beyond Apple's ecosystem.

Investigators also identified technical connections to Chinese-language developers and a Hong Kong-registered company called KeLing Technology Limited. The links included hosting infrastructure, code, and contact information, although the evidence doesn't conclusively establish who controlled the entire network.

Apple says developers changed apps after approval

Apple removed 19 apps, including Viefur, after reporters contacted the company and shared details of the network. Spokesperson Adam Dema said the apps complied with App Store rules during their initial reviews. According to Apple's account, developers subsequently changed the websites supplying their content, replacing approved material with pornography.

The explanation highlights a limitation of reviewing apps before publication. Developers can potentially change content delivered from external servers without submitting a new app version for approval, allowing prohibited features to appear after an app has passed review.

Apple also said it had suspended tens of thousands of apps over the previous year for similar bait-and-switch tactics. The suspensions extended beyond the identified network.

On October 16, Apple updated its guidelines to strengthen existing restrictions against nonconsensual intimate imagery and apps that conceal their functionality during review.

Guideline 1.2 now explicitly addresses AI-generated nonconsensual intimate imagery, requiring developers to prevent or remove such content. Guideline 2.5.19 clarifies Apple's longstanding prohibition against hidden, dormant, or undocumented features, including functionality activated after approval.

The changes strengthen Apple's existing policies, but they can't stop developers from changing content hosted on external servers. The company still faces the challenge of detecting those changes after apps have been approved.
